# Session 10: The Scroll

## Session Overview

### Creedal Statement

<!-- @include: LordsPrayer -->

### Key Elements
- **Key Passage** - Luke 4:14–44
- **Scripture Memory** - For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Hebrews 4:12
- **Catechism** - Q: What Christian practice enables Christians to minister to others? A: Word.

## Introduction

> All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.

<< 2 Timothy 3:16–17

The word of God … exercises the understanding of the wise … [and] it nurses the simple-minded. It presents in open day that which the little ones may be fed; it keeps in secret that whereby men of a loftier range may be held in suspense of admiration. It is, as it were, a kind of river … which is both shallow and deep, wherein both the lamb may find a footing, and the elephant float at large. Gregory the Great, _Morals on the Book of Job_

God's word is a sure and certain guide for life and godliness. Progress in Christian maturity requires increased attention and deepened submission to God's word as the ultimate source of all truth and the superlative standards for holy conduct. Unfortunately, many people build their lives upon shaky foundations. Those prone to shallow and misguided thinking can easily allow fashion, trend, and fad to sway their beliefs and lifestyle. Many yield to the changing tides of public preference and the shifting sands of popular opinion. The currents of contemporary culture can influence people away from God. Not all sources of truth are equal. Not everything loved by the majority is beneficial to humanity. Not everything under the name of spirituality is aligned with God. To experience the blessing of eternal life and to grow in the faith, we need to root our lives in a reliable standard of truth. Divine revelation to humanity, God's word is this trustworthy, reliable, and life-transforming truth standard.

The Bible is one of God's gracious gifts to humanity. This sacred book is an inspired, accurate, and trustworthy record of God's redemptive work in the world. It faithfully reveals his actions in the past and accurately unfolds his plans for the future. Although it is an ancient and historical text, it speaks relevantly to contemporary humanity. A testimony of unchanging truth, God's word is sufficient to address the ever-changing needs of sinful people. It is by God's word that we expose error and establish firm foundations for belief and godly living. The Bible guides us through moments of suffering, sustains us during times of doubt, and equips us for a life of ministry service. Above all, God's word reveals how sinful humans can receive divine forgiveness, eternal salvation, and gracious redemption. Through the example of Jesus, the Gospel accounts provide instances of a word-based life and ministry.

One such instance is found in Luke 4:14–44, where Jesus launched his public ministry. This narrative highlights the importance of God's word in the Christian life and ministry. At the beginning of the story, Jesus entered a synagogue in his hometown of Nazareth, where he read a messianic text from Isaiah. Jesus told the assembled gathering that he fulfilled the prophecy in this passage. After Jesus confronted the gathering for their misplaced messianic expectations, the people rejected Jesus and drove him out of the town. Jesus visited another synagogue in Capernaum, where he drove out a demon from an oppressed man. Soon after this, he healed Simon Peter's mother-in-law of a fever. After healing many people and driving out many demons, Jesus left the area to preach the gospel in other areas.

In this narrative, Jesus clearly rooted his life and ministry in God's word. He also demonstrated the power of God's word in his holistic ministry. Jesus taught in the synagogue, read Scripture, interpreted Old Testament prophets, alluded to key stories from Israel's history, and proclaimed the gospel of God's kingdom. Obviously, Jesus was familiar with God's word as a student of the Scripture, a teacher of the text, and a preacher of the good news. Jesus' miraculous deeds also highlight the power of God's word. Jesus used his own voice to cast out demons, silence evil, and heal sickness. In Jesus, we see a life devoted to God's word. Christian life and ministry are based upon a healthy intake of God's word so that there can be faithful output of God's word. God openly invites you to a life energized and sustained by the truth. God's inspired word is at the foundation of all spiritual growth. As you study this important biblical text, may you hear Jesus' teaching and heed Jesus' example for word-based faith formation.

### Biblical Commentary

<!-- @include: BiblicalCommentaryDirections -->

<!-- @include: NarrativeTheologyInfographic -->

#### Passage Introduction

##### Key Idea

God invites us into a life, faith, and ministry based upon his divinely inspired word.

##### Passage Overview

Reading the Bible is a foundational practice of the Christian life. Jesus' synagogue ministry, powerful exorcisms, miraculous healings, regular teaching, and gospel preaching highlight the power, authority, and priority of God's word. The Bible centers us in God's truth. It warns us when we stray. It is the firm and secure foundation of knowing who God is and what he has done on our behalf. The word of God unfolds to us the path of forgiveness, redemption, and deliverance. It reveals the true character of God, the sinful condition of man, and the gracious work of Christ's salvation. Grounded in God's word, we can navigate the complexities of an ever-changing culture with certainty, confidence, and conviction. God's Word is clarity to our eyes, wisdom to our minds, guidance for our feet, instructions for our hands, comfort to our hearts, refreshment for our spirits, and food to our souls. Modeled after the life of Christ, a disciple's life is word-based. Read the commentary to shed light on the scriptural narrative and expand your understanding of God's word and its role in your faith formation.

##### Passage Outline

#### Public Launch of Jesus' Ministry

> The Law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the Lord is trustworthy, making wise the simple. The precepts of the Lord are right, bringing joy to the heart; the commandments of the Lord are radiant, giving light to the eyes. The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever; the judgments of the Lord are true, being altogether righteous. They are more precious than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the comb. By them indeed Your servant is warned; in keeping them is great reward.

<< Psalm 19:7–11

> The manifold uses of the Holy Scripture grow clearer as we study the inspired book. It is the key that unlocks all perplexities. As Arthur Hallam said, it proves itself God's book, because it is man's book, fitting every turn and curve of the human heart.

<< Arthur T. Pierson, _The New Acts of the Apostles_

##### Introduction

Words matter. Human speech and communication form the basis of interpersonal relationships. What we say reveals much about what we believe and how we live. Our words determine much about our work and life fulfillment. Family life is built by the interactions, instructions, discussions, and conversations that take place in the household. The Christian life itself is a word-based faith. In his sovereign plan, God has chosen throughout the ages to reveal himself to humanity through the spoken and written word. God is a communicative being. He establishes a relationship with his people by revealing himself to them through his word. Throughout history, divine revelation has come in the form of law, narrative, history, dream, prophecy, and proverb. Today, humanity is the beneficiary of God's written and inspired word. The Bible is a faithful and accurate record of divine revelation—it is God's word to people.

Across all time and cultures, God's people are defined by those who base their lives on God's revealed word. Christians trust God's word as the standard of all truth and submit to God's word as an authority over their lives. In the Bible, people come to know the path of salvation, the purpose of life, and the basic principles for godly living. Jesus himself is called the Word of God. The written word of the Bible specifically reveals the truth about the Living Word, Jesus Christ. He is the fulfillment of God's revelation to men, accomplishing salvation for sinners and setting a perfect example for righteousness. There is nothing like God's word. It is reliable and relevant, an inerrant account of truth and a timely guide for life. As much as the Bible instructs us about our present life on earth, its overarching aim is to prepare us to inherit life in the world to come. Through the Scripture's own testimony, Jesus invites us to a life that is rooted, grounded, and established on God's word.

The story found in Luke 4:14–44 introduces Jesus' word-based life and ministry. In this narrative, Jesus read, taught, interpreted, and applied God's word in synagogue gatherings. During Jesus' synagogue visit in his hometown of Nazareth, he was eventually driven out of town after he explained God's word to the people. The character of divine revelation is highlighted through this account. Jesus used his divine word to drive out demons and heal sickness. These historical events and narrative developments give us insight into the nature of God's word. At the end of the story, Jesus spoke about the purpose of his coming: to travel around and preach the gospel to many people in various places. The purpose of Jesus' life and ministry emphasizes a main purpose of the Bible: to tell people the good news of God's kingdom.

A building without a solid foundation is subject to crumbling in minor tremors. A tree without firm roots is susceptible to falling in passing winds. An athlete without fundamentals is prone to make mistakes. In kind, a disciple of Jesus can only be firm, founded, and established when life is rooted in the word of God. In this narrative, Jesus taught God's word in the assembly, read Scripture in the community, used his words to silence demons, exorcised (cast out) unclean spirits, healed the sick, and preached the gospel. In response to Jesus' ministry of word and deed, people who crowded around him responded in amazement and astonishment at the power of his word. For Jesus and us, Scripture forms the foundation of life and ministry. We can encounter God's presence through Scripture engagement. Many faith practices help inculcate God's word in our lives: study, reading, dialogue, memorization, teaching, and evangelism. As we study this biblical narrative, may we practice God's presence through an increased commitment to God's revealed word.

##### Unrolling the Scroll: Reading, Studying, and Memorizing God's Word

###### Biblical Narrative (Luke 4:14–30)

After Jesus' temptation in the wilderness, he returned to Galilee. In the wilderness, Jesus resisted temptation, exemplified self-control, and overcame the attacks of the enemy. During this time of testing, Jesus utilized two important spiritual disciplines in his spiritual combat against evil: _fasting_ and _the word_. This latter spiritual habit is the main focus of this subsequent narrative. In the previous biblical narrative, Jesus went into the wilderness "led by the Spirit," and he resisted the enemy's temptations "full of the Holy Spirit" (4:1). Now, Jesus "returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit" (4:14), where he would publicly launch his ministry—a divine work that would be rooted in the word of God.

At this time, Jesus was growing in popularity and renown—"the news about Him spread throughout the surrounding region" (4:14). His ministry of _deed_ and _word_ formed the basis of his divine vocation. In his work, Jesus performed miracles, healings, and wondrous signs. Certainly, these extraordinary displays of power brought Jesus much attention. Ministering to people through his word, Jesus also spent much time teaching people the truth. While Jesus would instruct people in public, he also taught in the synagogues, Jewish religious centers for teaching and worship. Due to his synagogue-based teaching ministry, Jesus "was glorified by everyone" (4:14).

Eventually, Jesus came to the town of Nazareth, the place "where He had been brought up" (4:16). As was his usual custom, Jesus "entered the synagogue on the Sabbath" (4:16). The people and religious leaders attending the synagugue in his hometown would have been acquainted with Jesus as he grew up (cf. 4:22). Their familiarity made Jesus' next actions especially shocking. Following common procedures for synagogue worship, Jesus stood up to read a portion from Scripture (4:16). Often, a portion from the prophetic writings was read subsequent to the reading of the Law. Therefore, Jesus was handed "the scroll of the prophet Isaiah" (4:17). He found Isaiah 61:1–2 and read this before the gathering. This passage prophesied about the coming of the Messiah and divine deliverance.

Jesus read aloud to all those in attendance that God's promised deliverer would come in the power of "the Spirit of the Lord" (4:18). He would be divinely commissioned—"anointed" and "sent" (4:18)—to bring about God's salvation for his people. Specifically, the Messiah would announce "good news to the poor," "liberty to the captives," "recovery of sight to the blind," and "release the oppressed" (4:18). Although the divine work of the Messiah would involve miraculous healings, this passage distinctly identified his word-based ministry: "to preach" and "to proclaim" (4:18; cf. 4:19). A reference to God's eschatological work of renewal, grace, and restoration, the coming of the Messiah would constitute the "year of the Lord's favor" (4:19). In short, the coming of the Messiah would amount to fullness of divine grace to humanity.

Practicing Jews would have known Isaiah 61:1–2 well. It was a classic text of messianic hope that promised God's deliverance and redemption. Importantly, Jesus did not complete a reading of the entirety of this section of Scripture. He stopped in the middle of the passage, which reads as follows: "the day of our God's vengeance, to comfort all who mourn" (Isaiah 61:2). At this time, Jesus ended his reading of a text that focused on God's gracious redemption and did not mention the subsequent reality of God's righteous judgment. After reading this short portion of Holy Scripture, Jesus "rolled up the scroll, returned it to the attendant, and sat down" (4:20). Jesus' dramatic act caught the attention of the people. In synagogue worship, it was not uncommon for someone to offer a brief explication or exposition of a text that was publicly read. The people were captivated by what Jesus had read and done. In fact, "the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him" (4:20). Then, Jesus offered an explanation of this text: "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (4:21). Essentially, Jesus was telling them that the ancient promises for a messianic deliverer were fulfilled in himself.

Initially, the people responded favorably to Jesus' reading and commentary. The people not only "spoke well of Him" but also "marveled at the gracious words that came from His lips" (4:22). A messianic text announcing divine promises of liberty, healing, and rescue would have encouraged the gathering. The fact that Jesus was announcing the fulfillment of these promises further delighted the listeners. Nevertheless, their excitement was tempered by some uncertainty. They knew Jesus was "the son of Joseph" (4:22) and wondered how such divine fulfillment could be true of a person who had grown up in their town. At Jesus' next words, the people's eagerness would quickly turn to rage.

Jesus confronted the inner intentions of the people. Quoting a proverb, he explained how people would demand that Jesus validate his claim as the Messiah by doing miracles in his hometown. The proverb read as follows: "Physician, heal yourself! Do here in Your hometown what we have heard that You did in Capernaum" (4:23). Jesus knew that even if he performed miracles for his fellow Nazarites, they would not accept his messianic claim. Prophets were commonly rejected by the people most familiar with them. Jesus explained that "no prophet is accepted in his hometown" (4:24). Jesus further explained that prophets themselves were often sent by God to specific audiences. He then gave two illustrations of this from Israel's history to authenticate this claim. He showed how, although there were many widows in the days of Elijah, the prophet only went to one (4:25–26). Similarly, although there were many lepers in the days of Elisha, the prophet only cleansed one leper (4:27). This all amounted to Jesus refusing to perform an authenticating miracle in his hometown of Nazareth. After Jesus gave this explanation, "all the people in the synagogue were enraged" (4:28). Their marvel had turned to indignation. The people formed a mob and drove Jesus out of town and intended to throw him off a cliff (4:29). Demonstrating his authority and power, Jesus passed through the crowd unharmed and continued on his way (4:30).

###### Biblical Principles

<Accent>_Bible Reading._</Accent> In this passage, Jesus demonstrated the importance of reading the Bible. Both his life and ministry attested to this. This biblical text begins with Jesus reading from the scroll of Isaiah. This reading took place in the synagogue among a gathered assembly of other religious devotees. The text explicitly mentions that Jesus' attendance at synagogue was "His custom … on the Sabbath" (4:16). Jesus was knowledgeable of Scripture, substantiating the fact that his reading of God's revealed word had become a life habit. He demonstrated this when he unrolled the scroll of Isaiah and "found the place where it was written" (4:17). Through a regular encounter of God's word in life and ministry, Jesus knew God's written word. Jesus was familiar enough with Scripture—from a combination of reading and listening—that he could locate a specific passage that he wanted to read. Jesus' knowledge of Scripture exceeded mere navigation of the text. Later, Jesus alluded to two other biblical instances. Jesus used these scriptural allusions to instruct his audience. A faithful Jew and competent teacher, Jesus understood the meaning and intent of Scripture. Consequently, when Jesus read Isaiah 61:1–2, he was able to select a text that was fitting for the moment, even stopping the reading at an appropriate place. His understanding of the Scripture also enabled him to offer an eventual explanation of the meaning of the text.

Jesus commends to us the reading of Scripture. God's word is divinely revealed truth. It is the unerring mind of God communicated to humanity. It is a trustworthy record of God's acts in human history, a gracious invitation for salvation, and a reliable guide to godly living. Preserved throughout the ages, God's word is both timeless in its teaching and timely in its relevance. Reading God's words should punctuate our daily lives and distinguish our Christian fellowship. We should read the Bible individually and communally, privately and publicly, and intentionally and broadly. To faithfully read God's word is an act of humility, placing oneself under the authority of the inspired text. A regular and repeated habit of Scripture reading sanctifies imagination, builds attention, cultivates wisdom, and leads to Christ. In large part, a person's faith maturity is reflected in their habits of Bible reading.

<Accent>_Bible Interpretation._</Accent> This account highlights Scripture reading turned into biblical interpretation. Shortly after his public reading, Jesus explained what Isaiah 61:1–2 meant. In ancient synagogue practice, it was not uncommon for an explanation to follow the reading of God's word. Consequently, when Jesus told the assembly that the prophecy was fulfilled on that day (4:21), he specifically meant that he himself was the fulfillment of the messianic hopes expressed in this Old Testament prophetic text. Jesus told the assembled gathering what Isaiah's prophecy meant and how it was ultimately fulfilled in himself.

This is the basis of interpretation: to accurately explain the _sense_ and _significance_ of each biblical text, to move from _what the text says_ to _what the text means_. In addition to regular Scripture reading, believers should develop skills in faithful Bible study. Bible study requires precise attention to the details of the text. At its core, biblical interpretation is an act of observation, noticing what the text says on its own terms. To study the meaning of the text in this way honors God by elevating the divine character of the Scripture. God's people rely upon the Holy Spirit for enablement to understand, interpret, and apply Scripture—the divine author of Scripture (Holy Spirit) is the same one necessary to unlock the meaning of the divinely inspired text (cf. 1 Corinthians 2:10-16).

Scriptural study can (and should be done) personally and corporately. In this synagogue scene, Scripture interpretation took place through direct instruction and community discussion (4:21–27). Additionally, Scripture itself is its own best interpreter. After explicating the meaning of Isaiah 61:1–2 and addressing the people's misplaced expectations, Jesus alluded to two other portions of Scripture (cf. 1 Kings 17:1–24; 2 Kings 5:1–24) to substantiate his teaching. In these cross-referenced allusions, Jesus showed how moments in Israel's history revealed the purpose of his own ministry: to serve the outcast and marginalized. Observing the details of the text on their own terms, explicating the meaning of the passage, and correlating the interpretation to other Scripture is a wise and fitting way to study the Bible.

In addition to Jesus interpreting the meaning of the text, he applied it to the specific situation of his audience. Biblical interpretation should yield fruitful application. Biblical applications are textual implications that make demands on what people should believe and how people should live. God's inspired word shapes conviction and conduct. In the narrative, Jesus' actual pronouncement is important: "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (4:21). In this statement, Jesus affirmed that the ancient text ("this Scripture") has contemporary relevance ("today" and "in your hearing"). The prophecy from Isaiah had clear implications for Jesus' listeners—it impacted and affected them at a visceral, existential, emotional, and cognitive level (4:22).

By quoting the proverb and revealing their thoughts, Jesus applied his teaching to the people's conscience (4:23). Biblical interpretation is not simply the recovery of the historical meaning of an ancient text. On the contrary, biblical exegesis involves the intersection of sacred text and present-day existence. God's word has the inimitable ability to speak directly to us as nothing else can. We read the word of God like we use a mirror which exposes our flaws and shortcomings: exposes our misconceptions of God, our hidden sins, our malicious biases and prejudices, and our doubts and fears. While modern experience does not determine the meaning of the biblical text, no area of modern life or culture is left unaddressed by the timeless and trustworthy nature of Scripture. The Bible is relevant for all matters of belief and godly living. As such, we should rightly interpret the Bible in order to understand (and embrace) the right kind of life.

Jesus' audience understood and received his interpretation of the passage as "gracious words" (4:22). The prophecy of Isaiah was a message of fantastic news (4:18–19). The impoverished were offered a word of hope. Those in bondage heard a proclamation of freedom. Captives received a message of liberty. The blind were given an utterance of restoration. The oppressed benefited from a pronouncement of pardon. Those in search of God rejoiced at the coming of the Lord's bountiful favor. This prophecy from Isaiah highlighted gospel-centered themes at the core of Scripture: salvation, reconciliation, forgiveness, and freedom available to all who are ready to humbly receive them in faith. God's word is a refreshing and reconciling word to all who lament the burdensome weight of this broken and sinful world. More than addressing historical intrigue, the Bible is a message that offers us eternal life, ultimately found in Jesus Christ (4:21). We study God's word to become inheritors of eternal life and to know how to walk in this new life. Simply, the power of a reconciled and reconciling life is rooted and based in God's unchanging word.

<Accent>_Bible Memorization._</Accent> Jesus' familiarity with Scripture is notable in this text. Although he read Isaiah 61:1–2 from the scroll, he was able to recall details from the Elijah and Elisha narratives without a text in hand. Importantly, Jesus not only taught from a written text (4:16–20), but also cited biblical details from memory (4:25–27). Committing God's word to memory is a vital habit in the spiritual life. Memorizing verses, passages, and books of the Bible greatly equips us in the faith and contributes to our Christian maturity. Throughout the ages, Christians have hidden God's word in their hearts and minds through the spiritual practice of memorization. To be able to recall Scripture without text in hand is invaluable. It equips us for spiritual battle, it resources us to endure suffering, it outfits us for a faith journey, and it impresses God's word deeply into our inner person. <Callout>Internalization of Scripture should be the goal of all Scripture reading and study.</Callout> For God's word to so implant itself in our lives makes it become the operating principle for faith and godly living. The internalizing habit of Scripture memory assists in this larger internalizing goal of biblical application.

##### What a Word: Rediscovering the Authority, Power, and Grace of God's Word

###### Biblical Narrative (Luke 4:31–41)

After being chased out of his hometown of Nazareth, Jesus traveled to Capernaum (4:31). On the Sabbath day, Jesus entered the synagogue and "began to teach the people" (4:31). His instructive words were powerful and impactful. Similar to the initial response in the Nazareth synagogue, the people in Capernaum "were astonished at His teaching, because His message had authority" (4:32). Among those gathered in the synagogue was "a man possessed by the spirit of an unclean demon" (4:33). This demon exercised oppressive control over the man. In a loud voice, the demon challenged Jesus, scorning him with an exclamatory "Ha!" and expressing displeasure at Jesus with two confrontational questions—"What do You want?" and "Have You come?" (4:34). The demon expressed accurately who Jesus was—"the Holy One of God" (4:34)—but did so with brazen defiance and irreverent hostility.

With undeterred confidence and unimpeachable authority, Jesus "rebuked the demon" (4:35). Whereas Jesus earlier used his word to teach with authority (cf. 4:32), he now used his word to best an evil and demonic entity. The verbal rebuke came in the form of two imperatives: "Be silent!" and "Come out of him!" (4:35). Unable to defy Jesus' authoritative command, the demon threw the man on the ground before the crowd and came out of the man (4:35). Amazingly, no harm was brought to the newly liberated man. Once again, the crowd's reaction demands our attention. The gathering of people "were overcome with amazement" (4:36). They wondered about the nature of Jesus' teaching since his same commanding word had "authority and power" to drive out unclean spirits (4:36). At this time, Jesus' fame grew as "the news about Jesus spread throughout the surrounding region" (4:37; cf. 4:14).

After Jesus' teaching and exorcism in the synagogue, he visited the home of Simon (also called Peter). At this time, Simon's mother-in-law was gravely ill, "suffering from a high fever" (4:38). With urgency and desperation, they "appealed to Jesus on her behalf" (4:38). Jesus demonstrated compassion toward them and responded positively to their request. Similar to his exorcism, Jesus "rebuked the fever, and it left her" (4:39). So instant and definitive was this healing that Simon's mother-in-law "got up at once and began to serve them" (4:39). When day was coming to its end, Jesus performed many other healing miracles. People brought many sick people to Jesus. He laid his hands on them and healed them (4:40). Jesus also drove out demons in many who were oppressed (4:41). Many demons would attest to Jesus' identity when they were exorcised. The demons "knew He was the Christ" and would say, "You are the Son of God" (4:41) as they left the people they oppressed. Because Jesus did not want evil forces bearing witness to him, "he rebuked the demons and would not allow them to speak" (4:41). Once again, his strong and commanding word could not be resisted even by demonic forces.

###### Biblical Principles

<Accent>_The Character of God's Word._</Accent> A major theme of this narrative is Jesus' word (4:22, 32, 36). Scenes of teaching and instruction (4:14–30, 31–32) transition to supernatural demonstrations of power (4:33–41). The storyline of this early chapter in Luke is intentionally designed to highlight fundamental dynamics of Jesus' ministry, a divine vocation of proclaimed word and miraculous deed. The distinction and interconnectedness between these two modes of ministry are important. The narrative explicitly focuses on Jesus' speech, both his word of teaching and his word of deliverance. Significant to understanding the meaning of the text and the underlying dynamics of spiritual formation, this biblical text asserts that God's divine word is at the center of the Christian life and ministry. In this way, understanding the character of Jesus' spoken word helps us grasp the nature of God's written word.

In this text, Jesus' _supernatural works_ are a commentary on his _spoken word_. Jesus rebuked the demons when they confessed his identity (4:35, 41). He spoke a commanding word to exorcise the demon (4:35). He also employed his word to rebuke and remedy the high fever from Simon's mother-in-law (4:39). Not only did Jesus use his word to deliver victims of demonic oppression and bodily sickness, but the people themselves specifically reported on the power of Jesus' word when they witnessed his miraculous performances. When people heard Jesus' teaching, they were astonished because his teaching had authority (4:32). In the same way, people were amazed at the "authority and power" (4:36) when he drove out the unclean demon that tormented the man in the synagogue. These various textual details helpfully inform our understanding of God's word.

God's word is powerful (4:14, 36). Unique in content and character, God's word has the ability to overcome evil, heal disease, unfold truth, and transform human lives. God's word is sacred and inspired revelation (4:17–21). Because of its divine origin, God's word is living, active, and dynamic. Its dynamic power and divine origin mean that it is accurate, trustworthy, and reliable. An ancient account of God's past dealings with humanity, God's word is timeless and transformative in all generations and cultures. A record of historical facts, God's written word is also timely in its relevance to contemporary readers. Offering a trustworthy picture of the future, God's word enables us to steward our lives in light of coming reality.

In this story, Jesus spoke authoritatively—"His message had authority" (4:32; cf. 4:36). God's spoken and written word is also authoritative. To be authoritative reinforces the accuracy and reliability of the text but also highlights the spiritual demands it makes upon its listeners. God's word is a summons to belief and obedience. It makes exclusive assertions about truth, and it commands specific directives for godly living. Faithful readers cannot read God's word as a mere suggestion for casual consideration. God's word carries weight, enjoining its listeners to joyful acceptance, humble submission, and loving compliance. God's word appeals to conscience and conduct, calling people to faith and faithfulness. To read the Bible rightly is to receive it and to respond to it, to hear it and to heed it.

<Accent>_Gracious Deliverance and Righteous Confrontation._</Accent> As much as Jesus' synagogue teaching was characterized as "gracious words" (4:22), his commanding word of supernatural power was equally gracious. In effect, Jesus' exorcisms (4:33–37, 41) and healings (4:38–40) were a visible validation of his messianic identity prophesied in Isaiah 61:1–2 (4:18–19). The demonized man was oppressed. Jesus' word released him from his oppression and liberated him from his captivity. Simon's mother-in-law was weakened by a bodily sickness. Jesus healed her and restored her health. During his short earthly ministry, Jesus exorcised and healed many more than these (4:40–41). He paid attention to the multitudes of "many people" (4:41) and tended individually to "each one" (4:40). Kind and gracious, Jesus listened to people's appeals (4:38) and tended to their dire need. To the evil, Jesus spoke firm rebuke (4:35, 39, 41) and authoritative command (4:36; cf. 4:35).

That the events in this narrative take place on the Sabbath is also significant (4:16, 31). For the Jewish people, the Sabbath itself was a time to remember God's gracious provision, enjoy God's faithful presence, and look forward to God's promised rest. The Sabbath represented freedom from slavery, liberation from bondage, and deliverance from oppression. It was a weekly reminder of God's grace to his people and righteous judgment against evil.

Jesus used his powerful and authoritative word to extend grace to the needy and to oppose ungodliness and evil. Jesus spoke and acted in compassionate, kind, and merciful ways. His word met people in their moment of ignorance, illness, and oppression. He illuminated truth, preserved life, and overcame evil. God's word is gracious to bring deliverance, righteous to confront sin, and powerful to subdue evil. For those weak in body or spirit, God's word is a sure source of strength and courage. To the weary and oppressed, God's word is a reliable weapon of warfare. To the burdened and impoverished, God's word is a storehouse of riches and a faithful guide to God's presence. God's word reveals the pathway for salvation and deliverance and warns those who persist in ungodly rebellion. In all ways, God's word is the foundation for a vibrant and victorious life in this fallen world.

<Accent>_Teaching God's Word._</Accent> In this story, Jesus taught in various synagogues (4:15–16, 31–32). The text explicitly labels Jesus' synagogue attendance as "His custom" (4:16). At the synagogue, the Jewish people regularly gathered for a time of reading, worship, and instruction. Not only was God's word read in the synagogue, but it was also taught to those who attended. For Israel, God's revealed word played a central role in forming and shaping the community of faith. The same is true for the Christian church. Regular gathering with God's people is vital for a person's spiritual growth. The life of faith was never intended to be lived in isolation. One of the reasons why Christian fellowship is important is that it is in this context where God's word is taught. Faithful teachers are reliable guides to interpret, explain, and apply God's word. Certainly, believers should develop personal habits of Scripture reading and Bible study. But God also instructs his people to submit themselves to godly teachers who can accurately understand and faithfully expound his word to his people.

##### The Good News of the Kingdom: Preaching God's Word

###### Biblical Narrative (Luke 4:42–44)

Eventually, Jesus went to a solitary place. The crowds of people found him and tried to prevent him from leaving their area (4:42). Clearly, they had experienced Jesus' healing, authoritative, and powerful word. Nevertheless, Jesus would not yield to their request. Jesus told the people that he needed to "preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well" (4:43). Rather than staying in one locale, Jesus traveled other areas in Judea, visiting their synagogues and preaching the gospel (4:44). Faithful in life and powerful in ministry, Jesus submitted himself to a most fundamental work: the proclamation of the good news of salvation.

###### Biblical Principles

<Accent>_Preaching the Gospel._</Accent> In this biblical narrative, Jesus identified a major thrust of his divine vocation as a preaching ministry. The reading from the Isaiah passage focused on the proclamation of a message, specifically a message of "good news" (4:18) and "the Lord's favor" (4:19). At the end of the narrative, Jesus is depicted as an itinerant preacher. While people wanted to detain him, he spoke with conviction: "I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God" (4:43). Jesus' teaching unfolded the truth of God's word to people; Jesus' preaching announced God's saving work and coming kingdom for all who were willing to accept it. This preaching ministry was integral to Jesus' vocation: "That is why I was sent" (4:43). So important was this work that Jesus preached the gospel to many people in a variety of places. He traveled to preach "to other towns" (4:43) and "in the synagogues of Judea" (4:44).

Of course, Jesus' preaching of the gospel and the kingdom was essentially a message about himself (cf. 4:21). No one other than Jesus can deliver, save, restore, and redeem. Consequently, throughout this narrative, it is noteworthy that the news about Jesus spread (4:14, 37). Jesus did not stop these reports about him from spreading, but he did silence the demonic confessions (4:35, 41). While many people heard the news of Jesus and responded in faith, the demons had no intentions of pledging allegiance to Christ. Their accurate knowledge of Jesus' identity was insufficient by itself. To receive the gospel is to know Jesus truly and to submit to Jesus fully. <Callout>Gospel preaching is not merely a declaration about Jesus but an invitation to follow Jesus.</Callout> God's word confronts our most basic loyalties, offering salvation in Christ for all who willingly yield to Jesus.

To rightly read God's word is to sincerely receive God's word. In addition, faithful Christians take on the responsibility to speak God's word to others. Evangelism is a term that describes the work of sharing the good news of the gospel with unbelievers. All Christians are called to this evangelistic work. What Jesus modeled in his life and ministry is an example for us to follow. To be a word-based believer is to spread the good news of the gospel to as many people as possible. To personally experience the transforming power of God's word is motivation to publicly announce his offer of salvation to others. A life devoted to Christ is rooted in God's word, both in intake and output. A person well-grounded in God's word cannot help but be a mouthpiece of revealed truth to the surrounding world.

<Accent>_Responses to God's Word._</Accent> Throughout this narrative, people responded differently to God's word. The initial instance of Jesus' teaching in the synagogue resulted in Jesus' being "glorified by everyone" (4:15). When Jesus read the scroll of Isaiah in Nazareth, the synagogue gathering had their eyes "fixed on Him" (4:20). After Jesus revealed that he was the messianic fulfillment of the Isaiah text, the crowd "spoke well of Him" and "marveled at the gracious words that came from His lips" (4:22). Eventually, Jesus confronted the gathering, and they were "enraged" (4:28). They "drove Him out of the town" and attempted to "to throw Him over the cliff" (4:29). In Capernaum, people were "astonished" (4:32) at Jesus' teaching and experienced "amazement" (4:36) that he could drive out demons with his word. The demons themselves could not help but obey Jesus' word: what he commanded, they were compelled to do, even though they had no intention to pledge their allegiance to him (4:33–36). Those who witnessed the power of God's word spread the message (4:14, 37) and served Jesus (4:39).

This brief survey of reactions can be helpful to inform our own Scripture engagement. This narrative revealed mixed reactions to God's word. We must be careful not to read the Scripture in a dispassionate and uninvolved manner. To rightly read God's word entails a faithful response. When believers in Christ rightly engage God's word, it leads to worship, faith, obedience, service, wonder, and proclamation. Bible study should stir our affections to glorify Christ in all his majesty. Scripture reading should constantly fix our eyes on Jesus as the fulfillment of God's promises for salvation and forgiveness. Biblical teaching, instruction, and interpretation must call people to faith and obedience. Commitment to God's word should invigorate devotion to God in ministry and Christian service. Faithful study of the Bible also awakens our wonder and amazement toward God's beauty, power, and authority. To receive God's word is a privilege and a duty. We embrace God's word as the foundation for our lives and bear responsibility to announce his word to the surrounding world. In these ways (and more), the spiritual practices of the word should evoke faithful responses among God's people.

##### Conclusion

Jesus had a custom of attending synagogue for community worship. During these gatherings, God's word was read, interpreted, and taught. At the beginning of this narrative, Jesus attended synagogue in his hometown of Nazareth, where he publicly launched his ministry. He read a messianic passage from Isaiah and told the gathering that he himself was the fulfillment of the text. After Jesus explained and applied the text to his listeners, they became enraged and drove him out of town. Jesus eventually arrived in Capernaum, where he delivered a demonized man by exorcising the demon with an authoritative command and a direct rebuke. Later, Jesus also healed Simon's mother-in-law of an acute fever with the power of his spoken word. These miraculous works typified aspects of Jesus' ministry. In his ministry, Jesus healed many people and drove out many demons. This ministry served as a context for him to preach the good news of salvation and God's kingdom. Embracing his vocation with faithfulness, Jesus traveled to many places to preach the good news of the gospel.

As the Living Word of God, Jesus based his life and ministry on God's word. We, too, are invited into a word-based life and ministry. Immersion in God's word enables us to align our beliefs and worldview with God's revealed truth. Hiding God's word in our hearts can help us internalize the truth and apply it to our daily lives. In humility and submission, believers submit to God's authoritative word and benefit from its dynamic and transforming power. Believers can ingest God's word through reading, study, discussion, teaching, and memorization. Such biblical engagement is both a personal and communal endeavor. As we root our lives in God's word, we also bear a responsibility to herald God's word—to proclaim the gospel to people throughout the world. For the believer, spiritual growth and faith formation take place through the power of the Spirit-inspired word of God, a revealed word that announces God's good news, liberty, restoration, freedom, forgiveness, and favor.
